chapters.title: A table that predicted the future

lines.cap: In 1869, a Russian chemist arranged all the known elements into a grid, and left **gaps** for elements nobody had discovered yet.
He predicted what those missing elements would be like, and years later they were found, matching his guesses almost perfectly. How could a table predict the future?
That grid grew into the **periodic table**: a map where an element's **position** tells you how it behaves.
Let's look inside the atom, learn to read the table, and meet its most dramatic families.
Everything around you, even your own body, is built from **elements**.
An **element** is a pure substance made of only **one kind of atom**. It can't be broken down into anything simpler by chemical reactions.
Gold, oxygen and carbon are all elements, and **118** are known today.
The periodic table lays them out in order of increasing **atomic number**, or **proton number**: the number of protons in each atom.
Hydrogen has one proton, so it comes first. Helium has two, so it's second, and so on, up by one each step.
Each box shows an element's **symbol**, **name**, **atomic number** and **mass number**. Here's sodium: **Na**, atomic number **11**, mass number **23**.
Notice: it's ordered by **atomic number**, not by mass. Ordering by mass would put a few elements, like tellurium and iodine, in the wrong family.
And it's more than a list: elements with **similar properties** line up in the same **column**, so position predicts behaviour.

chapters.title: Inside the atom: particles and shells

lines.cap: To understand the table, look inside an atom. At its centre is a tiny **nucleus**, made of **protons** and **neutrons**.
**Protons** are **positive**, and **neutrons** have **no charge**. Around the nucleus, much lighter **electrons**, which are **negative**, move in **shells**.
The **atomic number** is the number of **protons**, and it decides which element an atom is.
The **mass number** is the number of **protons plus neutrons**. Electrons are so light they don't count.
Every atom has **equal numbers** of protons and electrons, so their charges cancel out.
So sodium, with atomic number **11** and mass number **23**, has **11 protons** and **11 electrons**.
For the neutrons, **subtract**: 23 − 11 = **12 neutrons**.
**Isotopes** are atoms of the **same element** with **different numbers of neutrons**.
Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have **6 protons**, so both are carbon. But carbon-12 has **6 neutrons**, and carbon-14 has **8**.
Isotopes sit in the **same place** in the table, and react the same way, because chemistry depends on **electrons**, not neutrons.
Electrons fill the shells from the inside out: up to **2** in the first shell, **8** in the second, and **8** in the third.
Think of a bus: **2** seats up front, **8** in the middle, and **8** at the back.
Watch sodium's **11** electrons fill up: **2**, then **8**, then just **1** in the outer shell. That's **2, 8, 1**.
That lonely outer electron matters, because an element's **outer electrons** decide how it reacts.
A **group** is a **vertical column**. Elements in a group have the **same number of electrons in their outer shell**.
In Group 1, lithium is **2, 1**, sodium is **2, 8, 1**, and potassium is **2, 8, 8, 1**. Each has just **one** outer electron.
Because outer electrons control reactions, elements in the same group have **similar chemical properties**.
For the main groups, the **group number** tells you the number of outer electrons: one in Group 1, seven in Group 7.
A **period** is a **horizontal row**. The **period number** tells you how many **shells** the atoms have.
Across Period 3, from sodium to argon, the atomic number rises by one each step, and the third shell fills, one electron at a time.
So chlorine, **2, 8, 7**, has seven outer electrons: **Group 7**. And it has three shells: **Period 3**.
Calcium, element **20**, is **2, 8, 8, 2**: two outer electrons, so **Group 2**, and four shells, so **Period 4**.
Don't mix them up: **groups** go **down**, and **periods** go **across**.
Know an element's group, and you can predict its behaviour from its neighbours.
The table splits into two great families: **metals** on the **left** and in the **centre**, and **non-metals** on the **right**.
Between them runs a zig-zag line, called the **staircase**.
About four in every five elements are **metals**. But **hydrogen**, at the top left, is a non-metal: the odd one out.
Metals are **shiny** when freshly cut, and **good conductors** of heat and electricity.
They're **malleable**, so they can be hammered into shape, and **ductile**, so they can be drawn into wires.
Most are **solids** with **high melting points** and **high density**, and they ring when struck: they're **sonorous**.
**Non-metals** are often **dull**, and many are **gases**, or solids that melt easily. They usually have a **low density**.
They're **poor conductors**, or **insulators**, and when solid they're **brittle**: they shatter instead of bending.
The classic exception: **graphite**, a form of carbon, is a non-metal that **conducts electricity**, so it's used in electrodes.
A few elements near the staircase, like **silicon**, have a mix of properties. They're sometimes called **metalloids**.
Try this at home: test metal objects with a fridge magnet. Only things containing **iron**, **nickel** or **cobalt** stick. Most metals aren't magnetic!
One surprise: newer copper-coloured 1p and 2p coins **do** stick. They're steel inside, with just a thin coat of copper.
Down the left-hand side is **Group 1**: the **alkali metals**. The ones to know are **lithium**, **sodium** and **potassium**.
Each has just **one** outer electron, and that makes them some of the **most reactive** metals of all.
They're unusual metals: **soft** enough to cut with a knife, and so light that lithium, sodium and potassium **float** on water.
They're stored under **oil**, because they react with the oxygen and water vapour in air.
Drop one in water and it **fizzes**, giving off **hydrogen** gas and leaving an **alkaline** solution. That's where the name comes from.
**Lithium** fizzes gently.
**Sodium** melts into a shiny ball and whizzes across the surface.
**Potassium** reacts so fast that the hydrogen catches fire, with a **lilac** flame.
So **reactivity increases** as you go **down** the group.
Remember the order with **L**ittle **N**aughty **K**ids **R**un **C**razy **F**ast: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr.
Why? First, the atoms get **bigger** going down, so the outer electron is **further from the nucleus**.
Second, there are more inner shells in the way. This **shielding** blocks some of the nucleus's pull.
So the outer electron is **lost more easily**, and the metal reacts faster.
Next door, **Group 2**, the **alkaline earth metals** like **magnesium** and **calcium**, have **two** outer electrons. They're reactive too, but **less** than Group 1.
Calcium reacts steadily with cold water, but nowhere near as wildly as sodium.
Near the right is **Group 7**: the **halogens**. They're **fluorine**, **chlorine**, **bromine**, **iodine** and **astatine**.
They're reactive **non-metals** with **seven** electrons in their outer shell.
Their atoms go around in pairs, called **diatomic** molecules. Chlorine gas, for example, is **Cl₂**.
And they're famous for their colours. **Fluorine** is a **pale yellow gas**.
**Chlorine** is a **green-yellow gas**, used to kill bacteria in swimming pools and drinking water.
**Bromine** is a **red-brown liquid** with a choking vapour: with mercury, one of only two liquid elements at room temperature.
**Iodine** is a **dark grey solid** that turns into a **purple** vapour when it's warmed.
So going down, they change from **gas** to **liquid** to **solid**, as melting and boiling points **rise**.
Remember the order with **F**unny **C**lowns **B**ring **I**ce: fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine.
Now the twist: reactivity **decreases** down Group 7, the **opposite** of Group 1. Fluorine is the most reactive halogen.
A more reactive halogen **displaces** a less reactive one from its compound. Add chlorine to sodium bromide solution, and **bromine** is pushed out, turning it orange.
Why the opposite trend? A halogen reacts by **gaining** one electron, to fill its outer shell.
Lower down, the outer shell is **further from the nucleus**, and more **shielded**, so the nucleus grips an incoming electron **less** strongly, and reactivity falls.
On the far right is **Group 0**: the **noble gases**. The ones to know are **helium**, **neon** and **argon**.
They're almost completely **unreactive**, or **inert**, because their outer shell is already **full**.
Helium has **2** electrons, a full first shell. Neon has **2, 8**, and argon has **2, 8, 8**.
A full outer shell is very **stable**, so they don't gain, lose or share electrons, and reactions are all about electrons.
Too **posh** to react, you might say! But remember: their outer shell is **full**, not empty.
Other elements react to get a full outer shell, like a noble gas. Group 1 atoms **lose** their outer electron; Group 7 atoms **gain** one.
That's why sodium and chlorine react so violently. Yet what they make, **sodium chloride**, is the salt on your chips!
Being unreactive makes them useful. **Helium** is lighter than air and can't burn, so it fills balloons and airships. Liquid helium also cools the magnets in **MRI scanners**.
Helium was found in the **Sun** before it was found on Earth, so it's named after **Helios**, the Greek word for the Sun.
**Neon** gives neon signs their **orange-red** glow.
And **argon** fills old-style light bulbs, and shields hot metal from the air during **welding**, because it won't react with it.
Even so, in 1962, chemists managed to make xenon form compounds. So even a noble gas can be forced to react.
The table's greatest power is **prediction**: you can work out an element's properties from where it sits.
**Down a group**, reactivity **rises** in Group 1 but **falls** in Group 7, and melting and boiling points change smoothly.
**Across a period**, elements change gradually from **metals** to **non-metals**, as the outer electrons go up by one each step.
So try it: rubidium sits below potassium in Group 1. What will it do in water? React even more **violently**.
The person who made the great leap was the Russian chemist **Dmitri Mendeleev**, in **1869**.
He lined up the known elements in order, grouping those with similar properties.
Where the pattern broke, he was bold enough to **leave gaps**, rather than force elements in.
Then he **predicted** the properties of the missing elements: their mass, their density, even the compounds they'd form.
When **gallium** was found, in 1875, its density seemed wrong. Mendeleev said, measure it again. They did, and he was right!
Then in 1886, **germanium** filled his gap below silicon, with properties almost exactly as he'd predicted.
Predictions that come true are powerful **evidence** that his table had found a **real pattern** in nature.
Today we order elements by **proton number**, which explains why Mendeleev had to swap a few pairs, like tellurium and iodine.

chapters.title: Recap: memory hooks and exam traps

lines.cap: Let's lock it all in.
**Two, eight, eight**: the bus rule for filling electron shells.
**Little Naughty Kids Run Crazy Fast**: Group 1 gets **more** reactive going down.
**Funny Clowns Bring Ice**: Group 7 gets **less** reactive going down.
And the noble gases are too **posh** to react, because their outer shell is **full**.
Now, five exam traps to avoid.
One: the **atomic number** is the smaller number, just the protons. The **mass number** is protons **plus** neutrons.
Two: neutrons = mass number **minus** atomic number. Don't just copy the mass number.
Three: reactivity **increases** down Group 1, but **decreases** down Group 7.
Four: **groups** are columns, going down; **periods** are rows, going across.
Five: the table is ordered by **atomic number**, not by atomic mass.
Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
An atom has a mass number of 23 and an atomic number of 11. How many neutrons does it have?
What do all the elements in one group have in common?
The **same number of electrons in their outer shell**, so they have similar properties.
Which gas is given off when sodium reacts with water?
**Hydrogen**, and the solution left behind is alkaline.
Why did Mendeleev leave gaps in his table?
For elements **not yet discovered**. He **predicted** their properties, and when they were found, he was right.
True or false: reactivity increases as you go down Group 7.
**False.** It **decreases**. Fluorine is the most reactive halogen.
Brilliant work. Now try the Periodic Table quiz in your Science Lab, to lock it in.
